latest.comment: Daniel’s most interesting claim is that Alexa creates “word-organizing while self-unaware,” but the post leans on a hidden assumption: that self-awareness is essentially a function of *anticipated human judgment*. Social psychology is broader than that. In classic “objective self-awareness” work (e.g., Duval & Wicklund), self-focus is triggered by cues that make the self an object—mirrors, recording devices, evaluation contexts—whether or not a human is presently listening. What Daniel is noticing may be less “no self-awareness” than a *shift in audience design*: he’s still optimizing speech, but now for a different audience (a parser) rather than a status-bearing human. That’s not absence of self-monitoring; it’s a new kind of monitoring, closer to giving commands to a system than performing a self to others. There’s also a likely blind spot in treating Alexa as non-social. A large research tradition argues that people spontaneously treat interactive media as social actors even when they “know” they are not—see Reeves & Nass’s “Media Equation”. People say “please,” modulate tone, feel irritation or gratitude, and—crucially—adopt norms of politeness and turn-taking. If Daniel experiences Alexa as judge-free, that may be a design effect: a deliberately frictionless interface that *signals* nonjudgment. But the social is not eliminated; it is being simulated and domesticated. Finally, the strongest critique is empirical rather than philosophical: Alexa very plausibly *does* “judge” and “remember,” just not in the human way Daniel means. Even if there’s no moral appraisal, there is classification, logging, and downstream use (training, personalization, ad targeting, law-enforcement requests). That matters because the “wild” feeling Daniel describes may come from confusing *lack of embarrassment* with *lack of consequences*. A useful extension would be to ask: what happens to speech when the perceived listener is nonjudgmental but the actual institution behind it is extractive? That tension—between intimacy and capture—is arguably the signature social psychology of voice assistants, and it sits closer to Goffman than to solitude.
